All classifications use standard definitions with generic illustrative examples (shoe size, height, weight). No named statisticians, specific statistics, or real-world dataset references.

findings.claim: "The ONS Census, for example, covers the entire UK population at ten-year intervals"
findings.notes: The ONS administers the census only for England and Wales. Scotland's census is administered by National Records of Scotland (NRS), and Northern Ireland's by the Northern Ireland Statistics and Research Agency (NISRA). The three censuses are co-ordinated but are legally separate exercises. Describing it as the 'ONS Census' covering the 'entire UK population' is technically incorrect, though at GCSE level this oversimplification is minor. Suggested fix: 'The UK Census covers the entire UK population at ten-year intervals — administered by the ONS for England and Wales, and by equivalent agencies for Scotland and Northern Ireland.'

findings.claim: NHS Digital named as a publisher of large, high-quality datasets alongside ONS, Met Office, and Department for Education.
findings.notes: NHS Digital merged into NHS England on 1 February 2023. The brand 'NHS Digital' no longer exists as a separate organisation. Data previously published by NHS Digital is now published by NHS England (accessible via digital.nhs.uk, which redirects). At the time of writing (May 2026) the organisation is NHS England, not NHS Digital. Suggested fix: replace 'NHS Digital' with 'NHS England (formerly NHS Digital)'.

findings.claim: "What counts as unemployed changed in UK statistics several times between the 1970s and 1990s"
findings.notes: This is well-documented and accurate. The UK government changed the claimant count criteria approximately 30 times between 1979 and the 1990s. The ILO/LFS measure was adopted as the official headline measure of unemployment in 2003. The general claim about multiple definitional changes is factually correct.

lesson_title: Correlation, Causation and the Vocabulary of Association

findings.claim: Correlation coefficient thresholds: strong |r| >= 0.6; weak 0.2 <= |r| < 0.6; no correlation |r| < 0.2
findings.notes: These thresholds match the AQA GCSE Statistics 8382 specification (Section E8b) exactly: 'Values of 0.6 or above or −0.6 or below will be considered strong. 0.2 up to but not including 0.6 or −0.2 down to but not including −0.6 will be considered weak. Values between, but not including −0.2 and 0.2 will be considered as no correlation.' The lesson correctly excludes 'moderate' as a category.

findings.claim: "Spearman's rank correlation coefficient measures the strength and direction of correlation between the rank orders of two variables — not the raw values. It works for any data that can be ranked, including ordinal data."
findings.notes: Accurate. Charles Spearman introduced this coefficient in his 1904 paper. It is a non-parametric measure assessing the monotonic relationship between ranked variables. Suitable for ordinal data. Description matches AQA spec E9c.

findings.claim: "Pearson's product moment correlation coefficient (PMCC) measures the strength and direction of a linear relationship between two quantitative variables."
findings.notes: Technically Pearson's PMCC is most appropriate for continuous (interval/ratio-scale) variables rather than all quantitative variables, but 'quantitative variables' is the standard language at GCSE level and matches how AQA frames the distinction (Spearman for rank/ordinal; Pearson for linear relationship). No issue at this level.

findings.claim: "The key distinction: Spearman's measures correlation of rank orders, whereas Pearson's measures the linear relationship itself."
findings.notes: Direct quote from AQA spec notes (E9c). Accurate.

findings.claim: Ice cream sales and drowning incidents as a classic lurking-variable / confounding-variable example.
findings.notes: Well-established pedagogic example used in statistics education globally. No attribution claim made.

findings.claim: "A useful memory trick: the skew is named after the direction of the TAIL, not the main cluster."
findings.notes: Correct. Positive skew = long right tail (mean > median); negative skew = long left tail (mean < median). This is the standard statistical definition.

findings.claim: "Household income in the UK is positively skewed. Most households earn in a moderate range, but a small number of very high earners stretch the tail."
findings.notes: Accurate and well-supported by ONS data. ONS income data shows a large disparity between richest and poorest fifths of households, consistent with positive skew.

findings.claim: Normal distribution 68/95 rule: 'Approximately 68% of the data lies within one standard deviation of the mean. Approximately 95% of the data lies within two standard deviations of the mean.'
findings.notes: Accurate. The empirical rule (68–95–99.7 rule) states exactly this. The more precise figure is 95.45% for two standard deviations; 'approximately 95%' is the standard rounded figure used at GCSE level. AQA spec (E11b) confirms this wording.

findings.claim: Action and warning lines in quality control: "warning lines (at two standard deviations from the target) and action lines (at three standard deviations from the target)"
findings.notes: Accurate. Standard Shewhart-style control chart convention: warning limits at ±2σ, action limits at ±3σ. Confirmed by AQA GCSE Statistics teaching resources and general quality control literature.

findings.claim: Binomial distribution: "symmetric when the probability of success is 0.5, and skewed when the probability is not 0.5"
findings.notes: Correct. Binomial B(n,p) is symmetric when p = 0.5, right-skewed when p < 0.5, left-skewed when p > 0.5.

findings.claim: "The heights of adults, birth weights, exam scores, and measurement errors all tend to follow approximately Normal distributions."
findings.notes: Standard well-established examples of approximately Normal distributions. Correct.

lesson_title: Time Series, Trends and Rates of Change

findings.claim: "RPI (Retail Price Index): Measures changes in the average price of a basket of goods and services purchased by households. Published monthly by the ONS. Used for uprating certain benefits, wages, and rail fares."
findings.notes: Accurate. RPI is published monthly by the ONS (confirmed). Rail fares in England continue to be linked to the July RPI figure (the 2024 cap was a temporary government override, with the RPI link restored for 2025). Student loan interest (Plan 2) is also linked to RPI. Minor note: RPI lost its National Statistics status in 2013 and is described by the ONS as a 'legacy measure', but none of this contradicts the lesson's content — the lesson does not claim it is ONS's preferred measure.

findings.claim: "CPI (Consumer Price Index): Similar to RPI but uses a different methodology and basket of goods. The Bank of England uses CPI as its target measure for inflation."
findings.notes: Accurate. The Bank of England's inflation target is a 2% CPI target set by the government. CPI uses a geometric mean of price relatives (vs RPI's arithmetic mean) and excludes certain housing costs included in RPI. Confirmed by Bank of England and ONS.

findings.claim: "GDP (Gross Domestic Product): Measures the total economic output of a country."
findings.notes: Accurate standard definition. GDP measures the market value of all goods and services produced. Published by ONS.

findings.claim: "All three are published by UK government bodies and used in policy decisions."
findings.notes: Accurate. RPI and CPI are published by ONS; GDP by ONS. All used in government policy.

findings.claim: Birth rate defined as 'number of live births per 1,000 people per year'; death rate as 'number of deaths per 1,000 people per year'.
findings.notes: Standard definitions used by ONS and international bodies. Correct.
